FOREWORD This Indian Standard was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Rubber Products Sectional Committee had been approved by the Petroleum, Coal and Related Products Division Council. Insoluble sulphur is an important form of sulphur used only in the rubber industry. It is not soluble When it is mixed in rubber, it disperses but remains in any type of rubber hydrocarbon. undissolved in the rubber. The use of insoluble sulphur prevents the development of a supersaturated solution of sulphur in rubber that occurs when rhombic sulphur is used. No sulphur bloom will develop on the surface of uncured rubber pieces when the rubber cools after mixing or At curing temperatures, insoluble sulphur rapidly processing; therefore, building tack is preserved. transforms to a soluble species, dissolves in the rubber, and enters into the vulcanization process. There are two general types of insoluble sulphur and the general description of each is detailed fo1lows: as

Low Insoluble Content Sulphur or Flowers of Sulphur - This product is made by vaporizing pure A select grade of this product sulphur and quenching the vapors in an inert gaseous atmosphere. contains between 30 and 40 perctnt of polymeric sulphur. This level of insoluble sulphur is often insufficient to prevent bloom, and its use is restricted to rubber compounds containing high levels Historically, this was the first of fillers or rubber compounds using modest amounts of sulphur. commercial insoluble sulphur available. High Insoluble Content Sulphur - ln this type of insoluble sulphur, the majorconstituent is polymeric sulphur. The polymeric sulphur level ranges from 60 to over 95 percent. The product is made by heating sulphur to temperatures greater than 160�C with subsequent rapid quenching. The polymeric sulphur content is increased by extracting thombic sulphur from the solid with an appropriate solvent. The amount extracted is determined by the particular insoluble sulphur specification. Insoluble sulphur also contains added oil and occasionally finely ground minerals. These are added to aid dispersion in rubber and to limit sulphur dusting. However, the additive levels are usually much higher than those used with rhombic sulphur. Oil treatments may range as high as .15 percent of the total material. Mineral additives may amount to as much as 25 percent of the final sulphur formulation. The treatment levels are always signiticant enough to require adjustment in the In this standard there are formulation to provide the necessary sulphur for complete vulcanization. two grades of insoluble ( amorphous ) sulphur namely Grade 1 - oil treated and Grade 2 - without Insoluble sulphur shall be treated with naphthenic oil for oil treated grade. oil mentioned. The Committee responsible for its preparation decided to prepare a new standard on insoluble ( Amorphous ) sulphur for rubber industry in the light of experience gained. A separate Indian Standard IS 8854 : 1994 `Sulphur for rubber industry' has been prepared. For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of final value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test in accordance with IS 2 : 1960 `Rules for rounding off numerical significant places retained in the rounded off value should be the in this standard. this standard is complied with, the or analysis, shall be rounded off values ( revised )`. ANNEX B [.TubZe 1, Item (vii)]
DETERMINATION OF THERMAL REVERSION OF INSOLUBLE SULPHUR

B- 1 PRINCIPLE The test sample is kept in a paraffinic oil at lOSaC for a fixed time and the amount of insoluble sulphur after the treatment is measured.
B-2 TOLUENE PROCEDURE B-2.1 Apparatus REk'ERENCE ( METHOD 1)

B-2.1.2

Thermometer 1OOT and 11OT.
Drying Reagents Oven

accurate to 0.2OC between

B-2.1.3 B-2.2

B-2.2.1 Paraffinic oil, viscous pharmaceutical grade, dynamic viscosity greater than 120 cP. B-2.2.2 Toluene -

Reagent grade.

B-2.1.1 Oil batb with thermostatic control accurate to f 0.2oc.

IS 14127 : 1995 B-3 PROCEDURE B-4 CALCULATION RESULTS AND EXPRESSION OF

Pour 20 ml of the paraffinic oil (B-2.2.1) into a 100 ml beaker, taking care not to wet the walls of the beaker. Put the beaker into the thermostatic bath (B-2.1.1) kept at such temperature that the oil in the beaker can be maintained at 105OC,control the temperature of the oil in the beaker with the thermometer (B-2.14, when its temperature is 105OC, add cautiously approximately 1 g weighed to 0.001 g (IV) of the test sample to the hot paraffimc oil and start a timing device. Stir continuously for exactly 15 minutes, then take the beaker out of the bath. Cool the parafinic oil -sulphur mixture to room temperature in a cold water bath stirring vigorously. When cold, add 30 cc of toluene (B-2.2.2) and stir well. Decant the paraffrnic oil/solvent mixture through a tared sin&red porosity P40 glass filter crucible (IV,) using a suction flask; wash the sulphur three times with 35 cc portions of toluene and allow to stand for 15 minutes after each wash before decanting. Using a spatula, crush any lumps of sulphur that may be found in the beaker; transfer all the insoluble sulphur quantitatively into the sintered glass crucible and wash 10 times with small amount of toluene.
NOTE - The sample must never he sucked completely dry before the last washing because reversion can occur due to the icing of the insoluble sulphur.

DETERMINATION C-O PRINCIPLE OF OIL CONTENT OF OIL TREATED SULPHUR

where w, = the mass of the tared beaker in grams,

C-O.1 Oil is extracted from the sample by using a solvent and the solvent is then evaporated off and the mass of residual oil is determined. Two procedures are specified, viz : a) light petroleum for rhombic soluble sulphur, and b) sulphur saturated hexane for insoluble sulphur. C-l LIGHT PETROLEUM ( METHOD I) C-l.1 Reagents on PROCEDURE

W, = the mass in grams of the tared beaker

C-2 SULPHUR SATURATED SOLUTION METHOD ( METHOD C-2.1 Reagents

C-1.1.1 Light petroleum 35-70 with a residue evaporation of not greater than 0.001 g/100 ml. C-l.2 Procedure

Weigh aboiit 10 g (W,) of test sample accurately on 0.001 g into a wide mouthed 250 cc conical flask, to which add by pipette, exactly 100 cc of light petroleum (C-1.1.1). Stopper and allow to stand at room temperature for 30 minutes swirling the flask every 5 minutes. Decant 75-ml oil the solution into a 100 cc beaker ensuring that no particles of sulphur are present and pipette 50-ml of this solution into another loo-ml beaker. Evaporate off the solvent from this SO-ml of solution by placing the beaker in a water bath in a fume cupboard. Remove the beaker front the water bath and allow to cool to room temperature. Extract the residue with 2 ml of light petroleum, measuring the solvent from a burette and adding it in such a way that the sides of the beaker are washed down. Swirl the beaker gently to disperse the residue with the solvent. Decant the solution into a tared (W,) 50-ml beaker. Repeat the extraction twice collecting all the washings in the SO-ml beaker. Evaporate off the solvent in a water bath and then in an oven at 80�C for 1 h in a fume cupboard. Cool in a desiccator and then weigh immediately (W,). C-l.3 Calculate following Calculation and Expression oil content of Results the

C-2.1.1 A solution of sulphur saturated hexane prepared by adding 60 g of rhombic soluble sulphur to 4 litres of hexane mixed well and allowed to stand for 24 h before use to allow excess sulphur to fall to the bottom of the vessel. Use only the clear supernatant liquid. C-2.2 Procedure

Weigh 5 f. 0.1 g of test sample (w) into a 2x)-ml conical flask to which add 25 cc of clear reagent solution (C-2.1.1). Maintain constant temperature throughout this stage of the procedure. Shake for IO minutes and then filter through a tared (W,) sintered glass filter crucible and wash the residue with 100 ml of the clear reagent solution (C-3.1.1). Wash the residue twice with 25 ml of ethyl alcohol. Dry the filter crucible plus residue for 1 h at 8O*C in an oven in a fume cupboard, cool in a desiccator and weigh (W,).
